clue.text: Shoulder, arms? A singular example

parts.note: read as weapons fired from the shoulder, and one single example of such arms; the drill command 'Shoulder arms!' is the decoy

explanation.surface: A parade-ground order, followed by a request for one instance of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoulder arms' looks like a drill-sergeant's command; here it means arms that are shouldered when fired, and the clue asks for one weapon of that kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A bazooka is a portable anti-tank rocket launcher rested on the shoulder to fire, so it is one shoulder weapon.

clue.text: American can write nonsense the other way round

indicators.note: says the two pieces appear in the opposite order to the clue's

parts.note: bull is slang for nonsense
to pen is to write

explanation.surface: An American can write rubbish backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb; it is US slang for a jail, and 'American' tells you the sense is American.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US a bullpen is a holding cell for prisoners, and can is American slang for prison.

clue.text: Girl with rising skill so captivated prophet

indicators.note: to captivate is to hold captive, so the girl and the skill enclose the other piece

parts.note: Zara is a girl's name

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: art is skill
thus means so

explanation.surface: A girl whose talent is growing has thus charmed a seer.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'rising' means read upwards; 'captivated' is the container signal, the girl and the turned skill holding 'so' between them. Zarathustra is better known as Zoroaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Zarathustra, also called Zoroaster, was the ancient Persian prophet who founded Zoroastrianism.

clue.text: Awards no marks

parts.note: O, nought, means no or nothing
scars are marks on the skin

explanation.surface: Prizes are handed out with nobody scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscars are the Academy Awards given annually for film achievement.

clue.text: Rural scene of Boxer Rebellion

parts.note: Boxer is not the Chinese uprising of 1900 but the loyal carthorse in Orwell's fable, where farm animals rebel against their human owner

explanation.surface: A countryside setting for the Chinese uprising of 1900.
explanation.walkthrough: The Boxer Rebellion was a Chinese uprising; here Boxer is the horse in George Orwell's novel, set on a farm where the beasts revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's novel is set on Manor Farm, where the animals, the horse Boxer among them, overthrow the farmer.

clue.text: Fly low, crashing into vessel

indicators.note: one piece breaking its way into another means it ends up inside it

parts.note: a vase is a vessel for flowers
to low is to moo, as cattle do

explanation.surface: An aircraft flying too low smashes into a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like a noun or an aircraft's action, but it means flee; 'low' is the cow's call, not a height.
explanation.definitionFit: To vamoose is slang for to leave in a hurry, and fly can mean to flee.

clue.text: See classical quartet's taken up instrument

indicators.note: in a down clue, taken up means read upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: lo is an old word for see or behold
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Look at how the string quartet's piece has been adopted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is the old exclamation lo, not a verb of looking; 'classical' signals Roman numerals. 'taken up' reads the whole run upwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A viol is a bowed string instrument of the Renaissance and Baroque, ancestor of the viola da gamba.

clue.text: When shine appears using pine wax

parts.note: to moon is to pine or mope dreamily
to wax is to grow or rise, as the moon does

explanation.surface: Polish shows up its gleam when you use wax on pine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shine' suggests polish on wood; it is moonshine, the light of the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: Moonrise is the moment the moon comes over the horizon, when moonshine first appears.

clue.text: Ribbon half-heartedly trimmed up for sash

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the remaining letters are read upwards
trimmed takes off the first and last letters, and half-heartedly removes one of the two central ones

explanation.surface: A ribbon is shortened carelessly to make a sash.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking R and N off the ends and one of the middle Bs leaves IBO; 'up' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: An obi is the broad sash worn round a Japanese kimono.

clue.text: Harsh words in print with no introduction about setter

indicators.note: with no introduction means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: text is printed words
re means about or concerning
the setter refers to himself as me

explanation.surface: A severe printed message without a preamble about the compiler.
explanation.definitionFit: Extreme means harsh or severe, as in extreme measures.

clue.text: Ancient instrument Louvre regularly exhibited

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means every other letter of the next word

explanation.surface: An old musical instrument is on display at the Paris gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: A lur is a long curved bronze horn from Bronze Age Scandinavia, an ancient wind instrument.

clue.text: I work to improve society's lowest members

definitions.text: I work to improve society's lowest members

parts.words: I work to improve society's lowest members
parts.note: the 'lowest members' are not the poor of society but the body's lowest parts, the feet, which this professional treats

explanation.surface: A social reformer describes a mission to help the underclass.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a charity worker helping the poorest people; the members are limbs, and the lowest of them are feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A chiropodist is a foot-care specialist, and feet are a person's lowest members.

clue.text: Fade quietly and endlessly? He never, never will

parts.note: to peter out is to fade away
p (piano) is the musical mark for quietly

indicators.note: endlessly means the final letter of the word and is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone asked whether they'll fade gently away insists that they never will.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the boy who never grows up, from the Never Never Land; the doubled 'never' points there.
explanation.definitionFit: J M Barrie's boy hero famously never grows up, so the clue's unfinished 'never will' is completed by 'grow up'.

clue.text: Ring of voice

definitions.meaning: on a dartboard the narrow band that scores three times the number is called this ring
the highest singing voice, especially a boy's soprano

explanation.definitionFit: Treble names both the triple-scoring ring on a dartboard and a boy soprano singing voice.

clue.text: British animals giving common cold?

parts.note: an ass is one animal
a monkey is the second animal

explanation.surface: Creatures in Britain are spreading the common cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cold enough to freeze the balls off a brass monkey' is a British saying for bitter weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass-monkey weather is British slang for extreme cold, from the vulgar saying, so it is an everyday term for coldness.

clue.text: Ant whose bite could make Adam and Eve red?

definitions.text: Ant whose bite could make Adam and Eve red?

parts.words: Ant whose bite could make Adam and Eve red?
parts.note: an insect that snips foliage could cut away the fig leaves Adam and Eve wore, leaving them blushing

explanation.surface: An ant's sting might leave the first humans flushed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red' looks like a rash from a bite; it means blushing, once the fig leaves are gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Leafcutter ants cut pieces of leaves to farm fungus, and Adam and Eve covered themselves with fig leaves.

clue.text: Evil doctor seen by American intelligence

parts.note: Dr No is the villain of the James Bond novel and film

explanation.surface: A villainous doctor is spotted by US spies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intelligence' looks like spies to go with the villain; it means common sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is British informal for practical good sense, a kind of intelligence.

clue.text: Hold on to sweets, Dad's expected present?

indicators.note: one piece is attached on to the end of the other

parts.note: afters is British informal for the sweet course or dessert
to have is to hold or possess

explanation.surface: Someone saves the desserts while guessing what father will get as a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: AFTERS is British for the pudding course at the end of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottle of scented lotion for the face is the stereotypical predictable gift for a father.

clue.text: Form resentment about extremely holy Saint

indicators.note: the first piece goes about, around, the others

parts.note: pique is resentment or irritation

indicators.note: extremely means the outermost letters of the word

explanation.surface: A form of bitterness surrounds a very devout saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' looks like a verb; it means bodily shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A physique is a person's bodily form or build.

clue.text: Show skill with restless desire before 7, say

indicators.note: the first pieces come before the other in the answer

parts.note: an itch is a restless craving
craft is skill

explanation.surface: Someone shows their talent with an urgent longing to get to number seven.
explanation.walkthrough: 7-down's answer is OBI, also spelt obeah: West Indian sorcery, so 'say' marks it as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Obi, or obeah, is a form of sorcery practised in the Caribbean, so it is an example of magic of this kind.

clue.text: Fit spin bowler bowled

indicators.note: to spin is to turn about, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: b is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled

explanation.surface: A fit spin bowler takes a wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' looks like an adjective for the bowler; it is a noun, a tantrum. To throw a wobbler is British slang for losing your temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A wobbler is British informal for a fit of temper or panic.

clue.text: Initially, American's secret intelligence aircraft lands in the east

indicators.note: initially means the opening letter of each of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: A US spy plane touches down somewhere eastern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lands' looks like the aircraft's verb; it is a plural noun, countries of the East.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is the continent of the Orient, whose many countries are the lands of the East.

clue.text: Bogus lower grades raised because amount is added on top

indicators.note: in a down clue the first pieces are placed above the other

parts.note: as means because
a sum is an amount

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means the letters read upwards

parts.note: D and E are low grades in exams

explanation.surface: Fake low marks were inflated because a figure was added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns DE into ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Assumed means false or adopted, as in an assumed name, which is a bogus one.

clue.text: Almost off-course line of Merak and Dubhe, say

indicators.note: almost means the word stops one letter short

parts.note: astray means off course

explanation.surface: Not quite on track along the line from Merak to Dubhe.
explanation.walkthrough: Merak and Dubhe are the two Plough stars that point to the Pole Star.
explanation.definitionFit: Astral means of the stars, and Merak and Dubhe are stars in the Plough.

clue.text: Loud brother on drug from 13

annotationWithheld.why: Loud brother on drug from 13 (6): BR (brother) and BRASS (from 13, BRASS MONKEY) are visible, but no reading of 'on drug' supplies ASSY or the final Y; scan matches and no source gives the parse

clue.text: Rob goes for unwanted snaps?

parts.note: to mug is to rob in the street
shots are goes, attempts or turns

explanation.surface: A thief takes a chance on photos nobody wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Police photos of suspects are snapshots no one would choose to have taken.

clue.text: Raise a boy

definitions.meaning: to lift with a lever device, as a car for a wheel change
a boy's name, short for John

explanation.definitionFit: Jack means to lift (jack up a car) and is a common boy's name.

clue.text: Ruth's to continue leading final phase

indicators.note: leading means coming in front of the other piece

parts.note: to last is to continue or endure
ruth is pity and quarter is mercy shown to a defeated enemy

explanation.surface: Ruth intends to keep ahead into the closing stage of a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruth looks like a woman's name; it is the old word for pity, which matches quarter as mercy.
explanation.definitionFit: The last quarter is the moon's final phase before the new moon, and the final period of a game.

clue.text: Blue movies ultimately viewed these days

indicators.note: ultimately means the final letter of the word

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, is the present era

explanation.surface: Pornographic films are what people finally watch nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue movies' suggests pornography; 'Blue' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue means sad or down in spirits.

clue.text: Kipling's book quickly read, ignoring introduction

indicators.note: ignoring the introduction means the opening letter is left off

parts.note: to skim is to read quickly

explanation.surface: Someone races through Kipling's novel, skipping the preface.
explanation.definitionFit: Kim is Rudyard Kipling's 1901 novel about an orphan boy in British India.

clue.text: South American worker who's quite right?

definitions.text: South American worker who's quite right?

parts.words: South American worker who's quite right?
parts.note: read 'South American' as from the American South, not South America: a sunburnt rural labourer whose politics are well to the right

explanation.surface: A labourer from South America is asked whether he is entirely correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South American' suggests Brazil or Peru; it means the southern United States, and 'quite right' means right-wing, not correct.
explanation.definitionFit: A redneck is a working-class white Southerner in the US, stereotyped as politically conservative, named for a neck burnt by fieldwork.

clue.text: Translated Early English died as passed on

indicators.note: translated means turned into a different form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: In Early English the word died is rendered as 'passed on'.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make it look like a translation note; the anagram of EARLY plus E and D gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Relayed means passed on, as a message handed along from one person to another.
